content.text:
I checked 13 claims against the record. None needed a flag: every one is backed by the record's lines or is stated as Code-Fix's reading.

- **The root cause stays unproven.** The claims about the scale-down window and the scaling loop all rest on F1, which is Code-Fix's reading of the configuration file. Nothing ran its test or its fix. The root cause field credits that reading to Code-Fix and calls it unverified.
- **Causal chain steps 3 and 4 are the closest calls.** Their own sentences have no hedge. I counted them as supported because each cites F1 as "in Code-Fix's words". Step 3 also rests on C1, the Investigator's observation that capacity kept switching between 3 and 6 cores. Raising the floor to 6 replicas was confirmed to fix the slowdown (T17–T19). If you read a citation as not counting as naming a source, step 4 should be flagged, because it states Code-Fix's account of why the autoscaler scaled down as fact.
- **The "what if" sentences weren't judged**, and neither were the action items. Only the facts in each contributing factor and in the went-wrong item were checked.

supported.quote: The production values for io-shop's HorizontalPodAutoscaler set its scale-down stabilization window to {F1.4} seconds.

As Code-Fix reads it, after scaling up from {F1.1} to {F1.2} replicas, the controller acted straight away on the lower per-replica CPU that its own scale-up had produced. It scaled back to {F1.1} replicas, where CPU was pinned again, so serving capacity kept flipping up and down instead of holding.

The shop's automatic scaling likely kept taking away the extra servers it had just added, because a setting meant to make it wait before scaling back down was set to zero, and that left too few servers to answer requests quickly.

While the scale-down window in the shop's configuration stays at zero, the autoscaler could again drop the shop back to too few replicas as soon as its floor is lowered, and responses could slow again.
Shop requests responded far more slowly than usual
People using the shop got much slower responses: its slowest requests took far longer than usual, while failed requests stayed within their normal variation.
Responses slowed because io-shop had too little serving capacity for the requests coming in.
It had too little capacity because the autoscaler did not hold the higher replica count. It kept taking the service back down to its floor of {T7.2} replicas, the count read at {T7.1}.

The autoscaler scaled back down straight away because the production values set its scale-down stabilization window to {F1.4} seconds. That let it act on the low per-replica CPU that its own scale-up had produced.
No check was seen that would have stopped a production autoscaler configuration with a scale-down stabilization window of zero from going out.
No alert was seen on the autoscaler repeatedly scaling io-shop up and back down. The fault was found only by the latency alert.
The alert fired on the production shop, but no on-call incident was linked to it, so nobody was paged.
